transcript.content: Hello, I'm Dr. Smith. It's nice to meet you; what brings you in to see me today?

Well, Dr. Smith, nice to meet you too, I suppose, though I wouldn't exactly say it was my idea to be sitting in this office today. They... well, my family and some of the folks from town, they insisted they bring me in. 

It all goes back to the county fair this past weekend. You see, I was scheduled to give my talk—I’ve been managing the ranch and farming that land for forty years, so they always have me speak to the community about the new equipment. It was a good crowd, too, sun was shining, a real nice turnout. But right in the middle of talking, I was looking at this big tractor they had on display, and I just... I had to show them. I climbed right up onto the tractor, right up into the seat during my talk, and I grabbed hold of the controls. 

I started jerking them, pulling the levers this way and that, because I needed to show the crowd the 'new pattern.' It’s this way things are supposed to move, you know, a whole new alignment. But they didn't get it. People started yelling, hollering at me to get down, making this awful commotion. And the thing is, Doc, I couldn't make myself stop. Even with everybody screaming my name and waving their arms, my hands just kept jerking those controls over and over to show the pattern. I couldn't stop doing it. So... that's why they packed me in the truck and brought me here.
Aside from the commotion at the fair, have you been hearing any voices or sounds that other people around you don't seem to hear?

Well, now that you mention it... yes, I suppose I have. But it's not like it's just random noise, Doc. It's very specific, and it happens out by the north pasture. You know the north pasture? It's the one that slopes down toward the creek, where the soil gets real heavy after a good rain. Anyway, especially near dusk, right when the sun is dipping below the tree line and the shadows get long—that's when it happens. 

I'll be out there checking the lines, making sure the pressure is right, and I start hearing these voices. Clear as day, Doc. Clear as you and me sitting here. And they aren't coming from the air, no, they're coming right out of the irrigation lines themselves. It's the strangest thing, but they tell me things. Important things. They tell me exactly which rows of corn are poisoned and which ones are blessed. 

And the thing that really gets me, the thing that makes me think maybe there's something to it, is that I hear them even when I'm feeling calm. You know, not all fired up and full of energy like I was at the fair. Even on the quiet weeks, when I'm just going about my business, sleeping regular, eating regular... I still hear them in the pipes. Just whispering about the soil and the water and what's tainted and what's pure. I tried telling my foreman about it once, told him to put his ear to the aluminum casing, but he just looked at me like I was crazy. Said he only heard water. But I know what I heard, Doc. I know what they're saying.

Aside from the energy you felt at the fair, have there been periods lasting at least a week or two where you felt so depressed or so high that it significantly changed how you functioned or how you felt about your life?

Well, now, that’s a big question, Doc, a really big question, because there’s a whole rhythm to farming, a whole cycle of seasons and feelings that go right along with it. You see, it’s not just the fair. There are times... well, there are these stretches, maybe a week, sometimes two or more, where I wake up and I step out onto the porch before the sun is even fully up over the ridge. And I look out over the valley, and I swear to you, Doc, it feels like the whole valley is just opening up specifically for me. I’m standing there with my coffee, and I’m just grinning. Grinning at absolutely nothing! Just the dirt and the sky and the feeling that I’ve got the energy of ten men. I feel like I could plow the whole south forty by hand if I had to, and I wouldn't even break a sweat. It’s this incredible high, this buzzing right under my skin.

But the thing is, and this is where it gets tricky, this is where folks start looking at me sideways... it doesn't take much to turn that feeling sour. Not much at all. I can be feeling on top of the world, but if one of the hired hands questions an order I give—say I tell him to check the fencing by the ravine and he asks if it can wait till afternoon—or if my wife, Mary, comes out and tells me I need to slow down, that I'm moving too fast and working too hard... well, I just snap. I don't mean just getting a little annoyed, Doc. I mean I snap like they’ve just insulted the family name, like they've spit on my grandfather's grave. I get so irritable, so furious, so fast, it even surprises me sometimes. My blood just boils over, and I'll lay into them, shouting and carrying on, when just two minutes before I was smiling at the sunrise. So, yes, I suppose there are those periods. It’s like being a firecracker, you know? All that energy packed in tight, just waiting for the slightest spark to set it off.
Are there periods lasting at least two weeks where you continue to hear those voices in the pipes, even when you aren't feeling that 'high' energy or that extreme irritability?

Well, yes, Doc, there absolutely are. And that’s the part that really gets under my skin, if I’m being honest with you. It’s not just when I’m buzzing like a hornet’s nest, you know? Like I said before, there are whole stretches—I'd say a good three, maybe four weeks at a time—where things are just... quiet. The weather’s steady, the work is getting done, and I’m just feeling, well, regular. I’m not snapping at Mary, I’m not waking up at three in the morning to redesign the tractor attachments, I’m just drinking my coffee and doing my chores like any other fellow in the county. 

But even then... even in those quiet weeks, Doc, when I’m feeling perfectly even-keeled... I still hear them. I walk out to check the irrigation, just a regular Tuesday afternoon, not feeling high or mighty at all, and the pipes are still whispering. They’re still talking to me, clear as a bell, telling me about the soil, about what's tainted. And it’s not just the pipes, either. During those same quiet weeks, I’ll be sitting at the kitchen table, looking over the farm data—the yield reports, the moisture levels, the fertilizer inputs—and I can see the hidden warnings in the numbers. Even when my mind isn't racing, I know those numbers are trying to tell me something terrible is coming to the crops. So, yes, the voices and the warnings... they don't take a vacation just because I'm feeling calm. They're there, week in and week out, no matter what my mood is doing.
